description: Solo dev project to build an interactive, accessible web solution for the challenge. Working independently on the design, development and presentation of the final delivery.
summary: In most space games, building a base is either trivially easy or students are stuck wading through dry textbook math. We created a lightweight C++ Windows app where students design a Moon or Mars habitat under a strict 25,000 kg launch limit, requiring them to make real trade-offs between solar and nuclear power, water and air recycling, radiation shielding, and growing food. When faced with a 14-day lunar nite or a Martian dust storm, players must reroute power on the fly to keep their crew alive, and see for themselves
details:
The Problem We Wanted to Solve

When students learn about living on the Moon or Mars, the hardest part of space engineering usually gets skipped: every subsystem steals from another. If you pack heavy metal radiation shields, you run out of rocket payload mass for water and oxygen. If you run a large hydroponic greenhouse to grow fresh food and boost crew morale, your power grid and water reserves take a heavy hit. We wanted to build a fast, tactile tool where middle and high school students can actually feel those push-and-pull constraints without needing an engineering degree to understand the interface.

What the App Does

Our application is a three-phase desktop simulator that puts students in the seat of a mission systems architect for a 4-person crew over a 30-day surface stay:

  1. Destination Selection (Moon vs. Mars):
    • Moon — Shackleton Crater ($89.9^\circ\text{S}$): Students deal with a 14-day (336-hour) lunar night where solar generation drops to$0\text{ kW}$and surface temperatures plunge to$-200^\circ\text{C}$, spiking habitat heater demand by$+8.0\text{ kW}$.
    • Mars — Jezero Crater ($18.38^\circ\text{N}$): Students face lower solar irradiance, a thin$\text{CO}_2$atmosphere suited for in-situ oxygen extraction, and multi-Sol global dust storms ($\tau > 4.2$) that cut solar output by$68\%$.
  2. Phase 1: Outpost Blueprint & Mass Budget Workbench
    • Every mission is locked to a strict$25,000\text{ kg}$payload mass cap (with a$6,400\text{ kg}$base habitat shell). If the player's design is too heavy, launch is locked until they trim mass or rethink their architecture.
    • Students configure four coupled systems:
      • Power Architecture: Lightweight photovoltaic solar arrays ($34\text{ kg/kW}$) + Li-Ion battery banks ($9.2\text{ kg/kWh}$) vs. continuous$10\text{ kWe}$Kilopower nuclear fission cores ($1,750\text{ kg}$per core).
      • ECLSS Life Support: Simple open-loop consumable tanks vs. a heavy, power-hungry closed-loop Sabatier & water recovery system (up to$95\%$recycling efficiency).
      • Radiation Shielding: Launched Aluminum-Lithium hull plating ($115\text{ kg}$per$\text{g/cm}^2$) vs. an In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) rover that sinters local lunar/Martian regolith over the habitat ($26\text{ kg}$per$\text{g/cm}^2$, but draws continuous rover power and reduces science bandwidth).
      • Food & Hydroponics: Freeze-dried rations vs. an LED aeroponic greenhouse that scrubs$\text{CO}_2$and supports crew morale at the cost of high lighting power and water transpiration.
  3. Phase 2: Interactive 30-Day Telemetry Simulation & Anomaly Interrupts
    • As the simulation runs at$60\text{ FPS}$, a live CAD-style cross-section schematic and three real-time telemetry graphs track electrical bus power ($\text{kW}$), battery charge,$\text{O}_2$and$\text{H}_2\text{O}$reserves, cumulative radiation dose ($\text{mSv}$), and crew health.
    • When realistic hazards hit—such as an X-Class Solar Particle Event (Day 8 & Day 23), Sabatier$\text{CO}_2$Scrubber Drift (Day 18), 14-Day Lunar Night, or a Martian Global Dust Storm—the simulator triggers an Anomaly Interrupt and pauses.
    • Students must act like flight controllers in Mission Control: using live power-routing sliders or emergency protocols to shed non-essential loads (like dimming greenhouse LEDs and pausing excavation rovers down to$15\%$) or overdriving the storm shelter and$\text{CO}_2$scrubbers to prevent a mission abort.
  4. Phase 3: Post-Mission STEM Engineering Debrief
    • At the end of the 30 days (or after a critical abort), the app scores the mission out of 100 and generates a root-cause diagnostic breakdown. It explains why the student's outpost succeeded or failed and connects their decisions to real NASA hardware.
